methods.dialog_description: Switching approach keeps the diagram, manual threats and decisions; only the analysis changes.

stride.name: STRIDE
stride.purpose: Review security threats to components and flows: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege.
stride.when: A good starting point for a web app or an API. Pitangus proposes threats by applying rules to the diagram.
steps: Set the scope: one feature (login, payments, file upload) before the whole system.
Draw actors, processes, data stores, data flows and trust boundaries.
Walk each element through the six questions; you don't need to come up with six threats per element.
Describe each scenario: who does what, to which asset, and with what impact.
Rate likelihood and impact, then decide the mitigation and who owns it.
Revisit the model whenever components, data, permissions or boundaries change.

s.name: Spoofing
s.question: Can someone pass as another user, service or component?

t.name: Tampering
t.question: Can data, code or messages be changed without authorization?

r.name: Repudiation
r.question: Could someone deny an action because there's no trustworthy record of it?

i.name: Information disclosure
i.question: Could data be exposed to someone who shouldn't see it?

d.name: Denial of service
d.question: Can legitimate users be kept from using the system?

e.name: Elevation of privilege
e.question: Can someone gain more access than they were granted?

tips: What applies to each element: actors → S, R · processes → all six · data stores → T, R, I, D · flows → T, I, D.
STRIDE isn't a severity: it helps you frame scenarios that you then assess in context.

linddun.name: LINDDUN
linddun.purpose: Find privacy threats: a person could be linked or identified, their activity detected, or their data used without them knowing.
linddun.when: Useful when your system handles personal data; it complements STRIDE, which looks at system security. It's a solid basis for a data protection impact assessment (DPIA).
steps: Mark which components and flows handle personal data in the diagram.
Go through the seven categories for those elements.
Describe each scenario from the data subject's point of view: what could be learned or done with their data.
Decide the measure: minimize, pseudonymize, encrypt, inform, give control or document.

l.name: Linking
l.question: Can data or actions from the same person be tied together, even without knowing who they are?

i.name: Identifying
i.question: Can someone tell who a person is from their data or activity?

nr.name: Non-repudiation
nr.question: Is a person bound to an action they should be able to deny or keep private?

d.name: Detecting
d.question: Can someone infer that a person uses the service, or that data about them exists, without actually seeing it?

dd.name: Data disclosure
dd.question: Is more personal data collected, stored or shared than needed, or with the wrong parties?

u.name: Unawareness & unintervenability
u.question: Does the person know what's done with their data, and can they act on it (see, correct, delete)?

nc.name: Non-compliance
nc.question: Does the processing comply with regulations and policies: legal basis, purpose, retention?

tips: Tag “personal data” in the diagram: without it, LINDDUN has nothing to work with.

pasta.name: PASTA
pasta.purpose: Analyze threats through the lens of business risk, in seven stages. It's broader and more formal.
pasta.when: For critical systems, or when the business needs to prioritize. It can be heavy to start with: apply it to a single feature.
steps: Objectives: what the system must achieve for the business and what must never happen (fraud, data leak, outage). Legal requirements.
Technical scope: technologies, infrastructure and dependencies; what's out of scope.
Decomposition: actors, components, flows and boundaries (the diagram) and the key use cases.
Threat analysis: who would attack and how. STRIDE serves as the threat library here.
Vulnerability analysis: known weaknesses tied to those threats (the findings from your scans).
Attack modeling: how they would chain together to reach a goal (attack trees).
Risk and impact: business likelihood and impact, countermeasures and residual risk.
tips: Stages 3, 4 and 5 fill in on their own from the diagram, the STRIDE rules and your scans; write down what can't be inferred.

attack_trees.name: Attack trees
attack_trees.purpose: Break an attacker's goal, such as “take over another user's account”, down into the different paths that lead to it.
attack_trees.when: For one specific, high-impact goal, when you want to see every way to reach it and which one to close first.
steps: Write the attacker's goal as the root.
Break it down into steps until every leaf is a concrete action.
Mark each group as OR (any one option is enough) or AND (all of them are needed).
Rate how hard each leaf is and mark what's already mitigated.
tips: The attacker's cheapest path is the one to close first.
An AND branch is cut as soon as one of its steps is mitigated; an OR branch only when all of them are.

attack.name: MITRE ATT&CK
attack.purpose: Look up and map tactics and techniques observed in real-world attacks. It complements a model like STRIDE rather than replacing it.
attack.when: To check the model against real attacks and review what prevents or detects each technique.
steps: For each component, review what MITRE lists for its platform (nothing is added automatically).
Add the relevant ones and note which control prevents or detects each one.
Mark it mitigated, or not applicable with the reason.
tips: Tactic = the attacker's objective at that point (the why); technique = how they achieve it.
Pitangus bundles MITRE's full Enterprise catalog, offline; the suggestions come from the platforms MITRE lists for each technique.

custom.name: Custom
custom.purpose: Combine STRIDE, LINDDUN, manual threats, PASTA, attack trees and MITRE ATT&CK as you see fit on the same diagram.
custom.when: When you need a threat modeling process tailored to your team or to a specific system.
steps: Pick the tools you want to use; you can turn them on or off without losing their content.
Draw the system and edit its components, flows and boundaries.
Review the computed threats and add your own scenarios where they make sense.
tips: The diagram is always available; the other tools are optional and saved with the model.

manual.description: Describe the scenario: who does what, to which asset, and with what impact. It's saved with the model.

manual.title_placeholder: e.g. Session hijacking on public Wi-Fi
manual.scenario_placeholder: An attacker on the same network captures the session cookie because…
manual.equivalent_hint: Your own severity keeps its name; choose a known level so it sorts and counts with it.

hints.objectives: What must the system achieve for the business? What must never happen (fraud, data leak, outage)? What do regulators or customers require?
hints.scope: Technologies, infrastructure, dependencies and vendors. What's out of scope for this analysis.
hints.decomposition: Actors, components, flows and boundaries are drawn in “Diagram”. Note the key use cases here.
hints.threats: Who would attack and why. STRIDE threats from the diagram show up on their own under “Threats”; add the ones you know from your industry.
hints.vulnerabilities: Known weaknesses tied to those threats: open findings from your scans appear below; add audits or pentests.
hints.attacks: How threats and weaknesses would chain together to reach a goal. Use attack trees.
hints.risk: Business likelihood and impact of each scenario, countermeasures and accepted residual risk.

help.title: How it works
help.add: Add components and boundaries from the canvas toolbar.
help.flows: To create a flow, drag from one of a component's connection points to another component. The arrow shows which way the data travels.
help.select: Click a component, a flow or a boundary's name to edit it here. Delete removes the selection.
help.colors: Color: each component takes the color of its role (legend at the bottom right); change it once selected. To name a color you chose, click it in the legend or use the field below the color picker. Orange ring: threats with evidence from scans. Dashed red line: unencrypted flow.

importer.ai_prompt:
Generate only a JSON object to import a threat model into Pitangus, for the system I describe. Return only JSON: no Markdown, no comments, no text before or after it.

Contract (the JSON Schema can be downloaded from the import dialog):
- Root: {"format": "pitangus-threat-model", "version": 1, "model": {…}}. model.name is required.
- methodology: one of {{methodologies}}. Include only that approach's sections; to combine them, use "custom" and list them in custom_modules ({{modules}}).
- ids: unique, lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, up to 40 characters. Components and flows share the same ids, so a flow can't reuse a component's id.
- References must point to ids that exist: a flow's source and target (two different components); a boundary's components (each component in one boundary at most); element in team threats, tree steps and techniques (a component or flow id); a tree step's parent (another step of the same tree, or null).
- Ids, references and types (text, true/false, lists) are strict: any mistake there stops the import.
- protocol: Pitangus knows {{protocols}}. Any other short text (up to 24 characters, such as "wifi" or "mqtt") is kept as written; Pitangus can't tell whether it's encrypted, so set encrypted.
- kind: Pitangus knows {{kinds}}. Any other value is kept as your own type; set custom_base ({{bases}}) to the role it should be analyzed as.
- data: Pitangus knows {{classifications}}. Any other short text is kept as your own class and counts as internal data.
- severity: {{severities}}. likelihood, impact and difficulty: {{levels}}. gate: and, or. ATT&CK status: {{statuses}}. PASTA stages: {{stages}}.
- ATT&CK: Enterprise technique or sub-technique IDs matching {{technique_pattern}}, such as T1552 or T1552.001. Pitangus includes ATT&CK v{{attack_version}}; a revoked or unknown ID is kept, with a warning.
- Don't include position, size, box, installation IDs or scan evidence. Repositories and domains go in repository_refs or asset_ref: they stay pending until someone links them.
- Add a description to flows and boundaries when it helps, and the model's assumptions as assumptions: [{"id": "a1", "text": "…"}].
- Your own values for severity, likelihood, impact, difficulty, ATT&CK status, category, kind, protocol or data class are kept as new options. Exceptions: a STRIDE or LINDDUN model uses only that method's categories, and a gate is and or or.
- Any other field you need is kept as a custom property, shown in the editor and the report. Pitangus also reads these synonyms as its own fields: {{aliases}}.
- Text is plain: no HTML. Names up to 80 characters.

Minimal valid example:
{{minimal}}

Current JSON in the editor (adapt it, or start from the minimal example):
{{example}}

create.title: New threat modeling project
create.description: A project models a system or a feature. You don't need repositories to start: link them later, one or several (microservices, micro-frontends), and propose components from them.
create.approach_hint: You can change it later without losing the diagram.
create.name: Project name
create.from_repos_hint: Pitangus reads their manifests (package.json, pyproject, go.mod, Cargo.toml, compose) and proposes each component, citing the dependency it comes from.
create.no_repos: No repositories match. Connect GitHub in Integrations if yours don't show up.
create.not_scanned_hint: Repositories that haven't been scanned are modeled the same way, but their threats won't show evidence until you scan them.

repos.nothing_new: Nothing new to propose from that repository: everything it found is already in the diagram.
repos.title: Project repositories

repos.ref_hint: Reference from the imported file; not linked

threat.evidence_repo: Open findings related to this threat across the whole repository; set the component's folder in the diagram to narrow them down. They're a signal to review, not a confirmation.
threat.evidence_paths: Open findings related to this threat in {{paths}}. They're a signal to review, not a confirmation.
threat.contradicted: Marked {{status}} by {{by}} on {{date}}, but the scans still find it: review the decision. It stays "with evidence" until they don't.

decision.mitigated: Say which control mitigates it (and where it can be verified).
decision.accepted: Say why the risk is accepted and until when.
decision.not_applicable: Say why it doesn't apply to this system.
decision.evidence_one: Note: {{count, number}} open finding points to it.
decision.evidence_other: Note: {{count, number}} open findings point to it.

elements.no_boundaries: No boundaries: flows don't cross any, so threats to data in transit are missed.
elements.no_flows: No flows yet. Data moving between components is where most threats show up.

values.custom_protocol_hint: Pitangus doesn't know this protocol, so it can't tell whether it's encrypted: check «Encrypted in transit» yourself.
values.custom_data_hint: Pitangus doesn't know {{values}}: they count as internal data and no privacy or credential rules apply to them.
values.custom_kind_hint: Pitangus doesn't know this type: it gets the threats of the role you choose below.

properties.title: Custom properties
properties.name: Property name
properties.empty: Fields of your own (an owner, a ticket, a review date…). An imported model's unknown fields show up here.
properties.structured: Structured value: shown as imported and exported as is.
properties.name_taken: There is already a property with that name: choose another.

context.assumptions_hint: What this model takes for granted: the provider's share of security, controls outside the system, what is out of scope. Every threat is judged against them; the report lists them right after what to address first.
